column5: I interpret use of AI to refer to current AI design and deployment practices. Fundamentally, such effects depend on choices made by AI companies (and businesses). There is a pro-worker AI path that would not lead to such unemployment effects, but that's not what is pursued.
column8: There are many claims that AI will impact high-skill workers. The evidence outside of coding is scant. AI will displace customer service and many other service workers. If displaced, high-skill workers may be able to adapt better to AI and take jobs away from low-skill workers.
column11: This is true even if AI does not affect high-skill workers adversely. AI is creating huge uncertainty about the labor market and jobs, and this will impact education.  AI in classrooms is also impacting human cognition and creating uncertainty about how student learning.

column8: Agree but tricky to tell WHICH workers.
column11: Agree esp if we are talking about very specific types of education such as law school as opposed to more general purpose education.

column5: It is too early to know.  Past technological innovations have not.  But this time could be different.
There will be substantial dislocation but I think people will find other jobs when AI is a substitute for what they are doing and in other cases it will be a complement.
I am more confident that inequality will rise (wages fall in the lower end) than unemployment rising.
Historically, labor displacing technologies sho up as declines in participation rates not an increase in unemployment rates.
column8: New jibs will be created.  But some high educated workers may end up moving down the job ladder if there job is displaced.

column5: There will be serious impacts of AI on the labor force but the impact on unemployment will depend on the sector and country. Many workers will suffer substantial wage loss. Older workers may retire earlier than planned. Unemployment is not indicative of long-run impacts.
column8: Many administrative jobs will be eliminated. Reimbursements at Stanford is increasingly burdensome. Bureaucrats slow the process with silly questions that have easy answers. AI bureaucrats may ask the same questions but they will be faster .... and cheaper!
column11: For 50 years I told students that math and CS courses will give you an advantage no matter what field you end up in. The big change is computers are becoming (as I predicted in my book in 1998) as smart as people. Being smarter than other people used to be enough. Not any more.

column5: Expect increased productivity to lead to more employment over time.  There may be short-term volatility.
column11: We will still need people to tell the AI what to do.
